en: What time does the bank open on Saturdays?
context: Asking a neighbour about bank timings.
explain: 'What time' asks for a clock time. After 'does', the verb stays in base form: open.
usage: Use it with a neighbour or friend before you plan a bank visit.
leelaQ: When do you usually go to the bank?
answer: I usually go to the bank on Saturday morning.

en: Which platform does the Chennai express arrive at?
context: Asking at a bus stand for the right bus.
explain: 'Which' is used when choosing from a limited set, like several buses.
usage: Use it at a bus stand when you are unsure which bus to board.
leelaQ: How do you usually find the right bus in your city?
answer: I usually ask the conductor or check the board at the bus stand.

en: How much is the auto fare to the railway station?
context: Asking an auto driver about the price.
explain: 'How much' asks about price. Ask before you sit so there is no argument later.
usage: Use it with an auto driver before starting the ride.
leelaQ: How do you go to the railway station?
answer: I take an auto or sometimes a bus to the station.

en: Who is the person sitting next to Priya?
context: Asking a colleague about a new face in a meeting.
explain: 'Who' asks about a person. 'Sitting' is a short way to say 'who is sitting'.
usage: Use it with a colleague at an event when you see someone new.
leelaQ: Who sits next to you in your office?
answer: My friend Karthik sits next to me in the office.

en: Why are you looking so worried today?
context: Asking a friend who seems upset.
explain: 'Why' asks for a reason. 'So worried' shows you noticed something strong.
usage: Use it with a friend or colleague who looks troubled.
leelaQ: What makes you worried these days?
answer: Exams make me worried these days.

en: Which bus goes to the Central market?
context: Asking at a bus stop.
explain: 'Which' is used when we choose from a few known things, like bus numbers.
usage: Use it at a bus stop with a conductor or another passenger.
leelaQ: Which bus do you take to your office?
answer: I take bus number twenty-two to my office.

en: Whose umbrella is this on the chair?
tamil: நாற்காலி மேல இருக்கற இந்த குடை யாரோடது?
context: Asking colleagues about a forgotten item.
explain: 'Whose' asks who owns something. Use it for any item you find lying around.
usage: Use it in an office or classroom when you find an unclaimed item.
leelaQ: Do you carry an umbrella in the rainy season?
answer: Yes, I always keep an umbrella in my bag.

en: How long will the repair take?
context: Asking a mechanic about the time needed.
explain: 'How long' asks about time taken. 'Will' talks about the future.
usage: Use it with a mechanic or a technician before leaving your vehicle or phone.
leelaQ: What did you repair recently?
answer: I repaired my phone screen last week.

en: How often do you visit your native place?
tamil: நீங்க எவ்வளவு அடிக்கடி சொந்த ஊருக்கு போவீங்க?
context: Chatting with a new colleague.
explain: 'How often' asks about frequency. Answers are like: every month, twice a year.
usage: Use it in a casual chat with a colleague from another town.
leelaQ: Do you go to your native place often, and why?
answer: I visit my native place twice a year.

en: How far is the airport from your house?
tamil: உங்க வீட்டுல இருந்து ஏர்போர்ட் எவ்வளவு தூரம்?
context: Asking a friend before planning a trip.
explain: 'How far' asks about distance. It is common with places and travel.
usage: Use it with a friend who lives in another part of the city.
leelaQ: How far is your office from your house?
answer: My office is about ten kilometres from my house.

en: Why is the bus so late today?
context: Asking a fellow passenger at the bus stop.
explain: 'Why' asks for a reason. 'So late' stresses how much delayed it is.
usage: Use it with another passenger when a bus or train is delayed.
leelaQ: What do you do when your bus is late?
answer: I wait patiently and sometimes book an auto instead.

en: Did you have your breakfast?
context: Greeting a family member in the morning.
explain: 'Did you ...?' asks about a finished action. In India this is also a caring greeting.
usage: Use it with family or friends as a caring question in the morning.
leelaQ: What did you have for breakfast today?
answer: I had idli and sambar for breakfast today.

en: Have you finished the report yet?
context: Asking a team member about progress.
explain: Present perfect with 'yet' asks if something is done by now.
usage: Use it with a team member when you need an update.
leelaQ: Have you finished your work for today?
answer: Yes, I have finished all my work for today.

en: Have you ever been to Kerala?
context: Chatting with a friend about travel.
explain: 'Have you ever been to ...?' asks about life experience, not a fixed time.
usage: Use it in a casual chat when you talk about holidays.
leelaQ: Have you ever been to a hill station?
answer: Yes, I have been to Ooty with my family.

en: Do you know how to reach the temple from here?
context: Asking a local for directions to a temple.
explain: 'Do you know how to ...' is a polite indirect way to ask for directions.
usage: Use it with a stranger on the street when you are looking for a place.
leelaQ: How do you ask for directions in a new town?
answer: I ask a local person politely or I use the map on my phone.

en: Excuse me, is anyone sitting next to you?
context: Asking a train passenger about a free spot.
explain: 'Excuse me' starts politely. 'Is anyone sitting' checks if a seat is free.
usage: Use it in a train or bus before you take an empty seat.
leelaQ: Do you like a window seat or an aisle seat?
answer: I like a window seat because I enjoy watching the view.

en: Do you know where the canteen is?
context: Asking a colleague on your first day.
explain: In 'Do you know where ... is?', we use normal order (the canteen is), not 'where is the canteen'.
usage: Use it on your first day in a new office or college.
leelaQ: Where do you have lunch at work?
answer: I have lunch in the canteen with my team.

en: Could you tell me how to reach the post office?
tamil: போஸ்ட் ஆபீஸுக்கு எப்படி போகணும்னு சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Politely asking a stranger for directions.
explain: 'Could you tell me how to ...?' is a polite, indirect way to ask for directions.
usage: Use it with an older person or a stranger when you are lost.
leelaQ: What do you do when you lose your way?
answer: I ask someone nearby or I open the map on my phone.

en: Would you mind telling me your name again?
context: Politely asking someone to repeat their name.
explain: 'Would you mind ...ing' is very polite. It sounds soft and respectful.
usage: Use it when you forgot someone's name and want to ask without sounding rude.
leelaQ: Do you forget names easily?
answer: Yes, I sometimes forget names after the first meeting.

en: Do you happen to know the Wi-Fi password?
context: Asking a host or a cafe staff member.
explain: 'Do you happen to know ...?' is a soft way to ask for information.
usage: Use it in a cafe, a friend's home or a hotel.
leelaQ: Do you share your Wi-Fi password with guests?
answer: Yes, I share it with my close friends and family.

en: I was wondering if you could help me with this form.
tamil: இந்த ஃபார்மை நிரப்ப நீங்க உதவி பண்ண முடியுமான்னு யோசிச்சேன்.
context: Politely asking a clerk for help.
explain: 'I was wondering if ...' makes a request very polite and indirect.
usage: Use it at an office counter or with an official when you need help.
leelaQ: Who helps you with paperwork?
answer: My brother helps me with all my paperwork.

en: Can you please tell me the way to the bus stand?
context: Asking a shopkeeper for directions.
explain: 'Can you please ...?' is a simple polite request used in daily life.
usage: Use it with a shopkeeper or passer-by in a new area.
leelaQ: How do you find a new place in the city?
answer: I use Google Maps to find new places.

en: Would you mind repeating that once more?
context: Asking a speaker to repeat something you missed.
explain: 'Would you mind ...ing' is a very polite way to ask someone to do something.
usage: Use it in a meeting or phone call when you did not hear clearly.
leelaQ: What do you say when you do not understand someone?
answer: I say, sorry, could you please repeat that?

en: May I know your good name, please?
context: Asking a visitor's name at a reception.
explain: 'May I know your good name?' is very common in Indian English at reception desks.
usage: Use it as a receptionist or when you meet an elder politely.
leelaQ: What is your full name?
answer: My full name is Arun Kumar.

en: Could I borrow your pen for a minute?
tamil: உங்க பேனாவ ஒரு நிமிஷம் கடன் வாங்கலாமா?
context: Asking a colleague for a pen.
explain: 'Could I ...?' asks permission politely. 'For a minute' shows it is short.
usage: Use it with a colleague or a classmate when you need something small.
leelaQ: What do you often borrow from friends?
answer: I often borrow books from my friends.

en: May I borrow your pen for a minute?
tamil: உங்க பேனாவை ஒரு நிமிஷம் கடன் வாங்கலாமா?
context: Asking a classmate for a pen.
explain: 'May I' is formal and polite for asking permission. 'Borrow' means take for a short time.
usage: Use it with a classmate or colleague when you need to use something briefly.
leelaQ: Do you often borrow things from friends?
answer: Yes, sometimes I borrow a pen or a charger from my friends.

en: Would you like some more tea?
context: Offering tea to a guest at home.
explain: 'Would you like ...?' is a polite way to offer something to a guest.
usage: Use it with guests and visitors at home or in the office.
leelaQ: How many cups of tea do you drink a day?
answer: I drink two cups of tea every day.

en: You are from Madurai, aren't you?
context: Checking a new friend's hometown.
explain: A question tag: positive sentence plus a negative tag. We use it to confirm what we think is true.
usage: Use it when you think you know something and just want to confirm.
leelaQ: Which city are you from?
answer: I am from Coimbatore.

en: It is very hot today, isn't it?
context: Making small talk about the weather.
explain: 'Isn't it?' is a question tag. It invites the other person to agree with you.
usage: Use it to start a friendly chat with a neighbour or a co-passenger.
leelaQ: How is the weather in your city today?
answer: It is hot and humid in my city today.

en: You haven't eaten yet, have you?
context: Checking before ordering food for a friend.
explain: A negative sentence takes a positive tag: haven't ... have you?
usage: Use it when you guess a friend is hungry and plan to order food.
leelaQ: What time do you usually eat dinner?
answer: I usually eat dinner around eight o'clock.

en: She works in your office, doesn't she?
tamil: அவங்க உங்க ஆபீஸ்ல தான் வேலை பண்றாங்க, இல்லையா?
context: Confirming a colleague's workplace.
explain: For simple present statements, the tag uses do or does: works ... doesn't she?
usage: Use it to confirm something you already half know in a conversation.
leelaQ: Where does your friend work?
answer: My friend works in a bank near my house.

en: The meeting is at four, right?
context: Confirming the meeting time.
explain: 'Right?' is an easy tag in spoken English. It asks the listener to confirm.
usage: Use it with a colleague to make sure you have the correct time.
leelaQ: What time is your next meeting?
answer: My next meeting is at three o'clock.

en: You will come tomorrow, won't you?
context: Reminding a friend about tomorrow's function.
explain: 'Will' in the sentence becomes 'won't' in the tag.
usage: Use it when you invite someone and want a sure answer.
leelaQ: Will you visit your relatives this month?
answer: Yes, I will visit my uncle this month.

en: They didn't call you back, did they?
context: Checking with a friend about a pending call.
explain: A negative past sentence takes the positive tag 'did they?'.
usage: Use it when you want to confirm that nothing has happened yet.
leelaQ: Do you call back when you miss a call?
answer: Yes, I always call back when I miss a call.

en: Do you have any plans for Sunday evening?
context: Making small talk with a colleague on Friday.
explain: Present continuous can talk about plans for the near future.
usage: Use it with friends or colleagues to start a friendly chat.
leelaQ: What are your plans for the next holiday?
answer: I am planning to visit my family and relax at home.

en: Where did you buy that bag?
context: Asking a friend about a nice bag.
explain: 'Where did you buy ...?' uses 'did', so the verb stays 'buy'.
usage: Use it as a friendly question when you like something a friend has.
leelaQ: Where do you buy your clothes?
answer: I buy my clothes from a shop near my house.

en: When is your sister's wedding?
context: Asking a colleague about a family function.
explain: 'When' asks about time or date. 'Is' goes before the subject in questions.
usage: Use it to show interest in a friend's family function.
leelaQ: Have you been to a wedding recently?
answer: Yes, I attended my cousin's wedding last month.

en: What are you cooking for lunch today?
context: Asking a family member at home.
explain: Present continuous with 'what' asks about something happening now or today.
usage: Use it at home with your mother, wife or a roommate.
leelaQ: What is your favourite dish?
answer: My favourite dish is chicken biryani.

en: How was your interview yesterday?
context: Asking a friend about an interview.
explain: 'How was ...?' asks for an opinion about something that already happened.
usage: Use it with a friend or sibling after an important event.
leelaQ: How was your day yesterday?
answer: It was a busy but good day.

en: Where did you buy this lovely bag?
context: Asking a friend about her new bag.
explain: 'Where did you ...' with the base verb 'buy' makes a past question.
usage: Use it to compliment a friend and ask where they shopped.
leelaQ: Where do you usually shop for clothes?
answer: I usually go to the market near my house or shop online.

en: How long have you been waiting here?
context: Asking someone waiting in a queue at a bank.
explain: 'How long have you been ...ing' asks about a period of time up to now.
usage: Use it with another person in a queue or waiting room.
leelaQ: How do you feel when you wait in a long queue?
answer: I feel a little bored, so I check my phone.

en: Which one do you prefer, tea or coffee?
tamil: டீ, காபி ரெண்டுல நீங்க எதை விரும்புவீங்க?
context: Asking a guest for a choice.
explain: 'Which one ... or ...?' offers two choices. 'Prefer' means like more.
usage: Use it at home or in the office when you serve a drink.
leelaQ: Which one do you prefer in the morning?
answer: I prefer filter coffee in the morning.

en: Is there a pharmacy nearby?
context: Asking a local for help.
explain: 'Is there ...?' asks if something exists in a place.
usage: Use it with a local person when you need medicine in a new area.
leelaQ: Is there a hospital near your house?
answer: Yes, there is a big hospital near my house.

en: Are there any seats left for the evening show?
tamil: ஈவ்னிங் ஷோவுக்கு டிக்கெட் ஏதாவது மீதி இருக்கா?
context: Asking at a cinema counter.
explain: 'Are there any ...?' is used for plural things. 'Left' means still available.
usage: Use it at a ticket counter before buying tickets.
leelaQ: How often do you watch movies in a theatre?
answer: I watch a movie in a theatre once a month.

en: Do you have change for five hundred rupees?
context: Asking a shopkeeper for change.
explain: 'Change' here means smaller notes and coins. This is common in daily Indian life.
usage: Use it with a shopkeeper, auto driver or conductor.
leelaQ: Do you pay by cash or by UPI?
answer: I mostly pay by UPI these days.

en: Could you tell me where the restroom is?
context: Asking a mall staff member for the restroom.
explain: 'Could you tell me where ... is' is an indirect question, so use normal word order.
usage: Use it in malls, offices or hotels when you need the restroom.
leelaQ: What do you do when you cannot find a place in a mall?
answer: I ask the staff at the help desk to guide me.

en: What is the status of my order?
context: Calling customer care about a delayed order.
explain: 'Status' means the present condition. It is common in customer care calls.
usage: Use it on a call or chat with customer support about a delivery.
leelaQ: Have you ever had a late delivery?
answer: Yes, my parcel came three days late once.

en: When will my parcel be delivered?
context: Asking a courier person.
explain: A passive question: 'will ... be delivered' focuses on the parcel, not the person.
usage: Use it with a courier service or an online shop helpline.
leelaQ: What was the last thing you ordered online?
answer: I ordered a pair of shoes online last week.

en: Could you check if my payment went through?
context: Asking a bank or shop staff.
explain: 'Went through' means a payment was successful. 'Could you check if ...' is polite.
usage: Use it at a shop or a bank when a payment fails on your phone.
leelaQ: What do you do when a payment fails?
answer: I wait a few minutes and then try again.

en: Excuse me, is this the right queue for tickets?
context: Asking at a railway counter.
explain: 'Excuse me' opens the question politely. 'Queue' means a line of people.
usage: Use it at a railway station, bank or temple when you are unsure.
leelaQ: Do you like standing in a queue?
answer: No, I do not like waiting in long queues.

en: How many people are coming for dinner?
context: Asking a family member before cooking.
explain: 'How many' is for things we can count, like people.
usage: Use it at home before a function or when guests are visiting.
leelaQ: Who comes to your house for dinner often?
answer: My cousins come for dinner almost every Sunday.

en: How much time do we have before the train leaves?
tamil: ட்ரெயின் கிளம்ப இன்னும் எவ்வளவு நேரம் இருக்கு?
context: Asking a travel partner at the station.
explain: 'How much time' asks for the amount of time left. 'Time' is uncountable.
usage: Use it with family or friends when you reach a station early or late.
leelaQ: Do you reach the station early or just in time?
answer: I always reach the station early.

en: Why didn't you pick up my call?
context: Asking a friend about a missed call.
explain: 'Why didn't you ...?' asks the reason for something that did not happen.
usage: Use it with a close friend or family member after missing their call.
leelaQ: Why do you sometimes miss calls?
answer: I keep my phone on silent when I am busy.

en: Why is the internet so slow today?
tamil: இன்னைக்கு இன்டர்நெட் ஏன் இவ்வளவு ஸ்லோவா இருக்கு?
context: Complaining to a colleague.
explain: 'Why is ... so slow?' is a common way to share a small problem.
usage: Use it with a colleague or family member when the network is bad.
leelaQ: What do you do when the internet is slow?
answer: I restart the router and wait a few minutes.

en: What are you up to this weekend?
tamil: இந்த வார கடைசில நீங்க என்ன பண்ணப் போறீங்க?
context: Chatting with a friend on Friday.
explain: 'What are you up to?' is a casual way to ask about plans or activities.
usage: Use it with friends and colleagues on a Friday.
leelaQ: What are your plans for this weekend?
answer: I plan to visit my grandparents this weekend.

en: Where are you going for your holidays?
context: Asking a colleague about leave plans.
explain: Present continuous with a future time word talks about plans.
usage: Use it with colleagues before a long weekend or festival.
leelaQ: Where would you like to go for a holiday?
answer: I would like to visit Munnar for a holiday.

en: What should I bring for the picnic?
context: Asking a friend who is organising.
explain: 'What should I ...?' asks for advice or a suggestion.
usage: Use it with the organiser of a trip, party or function.
leelaQ: What do you take on a picnic?
answer: I take snacks, water and a small mat.

en: Do I need to carry my ID card?
tamil: நான் என் ஐடி கார்டு எடுத்துட்டு வரணுமா?
context: Asking a friend or a colleague.
explain: 'Do I need to ...?' asks if something is required.
usage: Use it before an exam, an interview or a visit to a secure place.
leelaQ: What documents do you carry to the office?
answer: I carry my ID card and my laptop bag.

en: How can I get a duplicate bill?
context: Asking a shop's customer care.
explain: 'How can I ...?' asks for the method or steps to do something.
usage: Use it with a shop or a service centre when you lose a bill.
leelaQ: Do you keep your bills safely?
answer: Yes, I keep all my bills in a file.

en: What is the best way to learn English quickly?
tamil: இங்கிலீஷை சீக்கிரம் கத்துக்க சிறந்த வழி என்ன?
context: Asking a teacher for advice.
explain: 'What is the best way to ...?' asks for advice. 'Quickly' is an adverb.
usage: Use it with a teacher, a senior or a friend who speaks English well.
leelaQ: How do you practise English every day?
answer: I speak English for ten minutes every day.

en: Is it possible to change my seat?
context: Asking at a bus or flight counter.
explain: 'Is it possible to ...?' is a polite way to ask if something can be done.
usage: Use it with a conductor, a booking agent or a cabin crew member.
leelaQ: What seat do you like in a train?
answer: I like a lower berth in a train.

en: Do you mind if I open the window?
context: Asking a co-passenger politely.
explain: 'Do you mind if I ...?' asks permission. 'No' means it is fine for them.
usage: Use it in a bus, car or room with other people.
leelaQ: Do you like fresh air in a room?
answer: Yes, I like to keep the windows open.

en: Could you let me know when the manager arrives?
context: Asking a receptionist.
explain: 'Let me know' means 'tell me'. 'When the manager arrives' uses present for a future event.
usage: Use it with a receptionist, a peon or a team member.
leelaQ: Who do you wait for at your office?
answer: I wait for my manager to approve my leave.

en: Would it be possible to reschedule our meeting?
context: Asking a client politely.
explain: 'Would it be possible to ...?' is formal and polite. 'Reschedule' means change the time.
usage: Use it in an email or call with a client or a manager.
leelaQ: Have you ever missed a meeting?
answer: Yes, I missed one meeting because of traffic.

en: Can you tell me when the next train leaves?
tamil: அடுத்த ரயில் எப்போ கிளம்பும்னு சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Asking at the railway enquiry counter.
explain: An indirect question keeps statement order: 'when the next train leaves'.
usage: Use it at a station counter or with a staff member for timings.
leelaQ: How do you check train timings?
answer: I check the app on my phone or ask at the enquiry counter.

en: Can you tell me what this medicine is for?
context: Asking a pharmacist.
explain: 'What this medicine is for' is an indirect question, so the order is normal.
usage: Use it with a pharmacist or doctor when you are unsure about a medicine.
leelaQ: What do you do when you have a headache?
answer: I rest for a while and drink some water.

en: Does anyone know how to fix this printer?
tamil: இந்த பிரிண்டரை எப்படி சரிபண்றதுன்னு யாருக்காவது தெரியுமா?
context: Asking a group in the office.
explain: 'Does anyone know ...?' is a good way to ask a group for help.
usage: Use it in the office when a machine stops working.
leelaQ: What office machine often gives you trouble?
answer: The printer often gives us trouble.

en: Has anyone seen my umbrella around here?
context: Looking for a lost umbrella in the office.
explain: Present perfect 'has anyone seen' asks about a recent action with a result now.
usage: Use it in an office or at home when you cannot find your thing.
leelaQ: What do you do when you lose something?
answer: I search carefully and ask my family or colleagues.

en: Did anyone call while I was in the meeting?
context: Asking a colleague after a meeting.
explain: Past simple 'did anyone call' with 'while I was' shows two actions at one time.
usage: Use it with a colleague or a receptionist when you return to your desk.
leelaQ: What do you do when you miss important calls?
answer: I check my phone and call back soon.

en: Who is in charge of the training session?
context: Asking a colleague.
explain: 'In charge of' means responsible for something.
usage: Use it in the office when you want to find the right person.
leelaQ: Who is in charge at your home?
answer: My mother is in charge of our home.

en: What is the deadline for submitting the form?
context: Asking an office clerk.
explain: 'Deadline' is the last time to finish something. 'For submitting' uses -ing after a preposition.
usage: Use it with an admin staff member or a college clerk.
leelaQ: Do you finish work before the deadline?
answer: Yes, I try to finish work before the deadline.

en: Which documents do I need to bring?
context: Asking at a government office.
explain: 'Which documents' asks about a choice from known items.
usage: Use it on the phone or at a counter before you visit an office.
leelaQ: Which documents do you keep in your bag?
answer: I keep my ID card and my certificates.

en: When can I collect my certificate?
context: Asking a college office.
explain: 'When can I ...?' asks about the time something is possible.
usage: Use it at a college, school or government office.
leelaQ: What certificate do you need soon?
answer: I need a salary certificate for a bank loan.

en: How do I get to the beach from here?
context: Asking a local in Chennai.
explain: 'How do I get to ...?' is the standard direction question.
usage: Use it with a local person or a bus conductor.
leelaQ: How do you reach your favourite place?
answer: I take a bus and then walk for ten minutes.

en: Is this the right platform for the Madurai train?
context: Asking at a railway station.
explain: 'Right' means correct. This is a handy question at a busy station.
usage: Use it at a railway station if you are confused about the platform.
leelaQ: Have you travelled by train alone?
answer: Yes, I travelled to Madurai alone last year.

en: What time does the first bus leave?
context: Asking at a bus stand.
explain: Timetable facts use the simple present: leave, arrive, open, close.
usage: Use it at an enquiry counter at a bus stand.
leelaQ: Do you like to travel early in the morning?
answer: Yes, I like early morning travel as roads are empty.

en: Is parking available near the hotel?
context: Calling a hotel before travelling by car.
explain: 'Is ... available' is a polite way to ask whether something can be used.
usage: Use it on the phone with a hotel or a hall before you drive there.
leelaQ: Do you prefer travelling by car or by train?
answer: I prefer the train because it is comfortable and cheap.

en: Does this restaurant serve pure vegetarian food?
tamil: இந்த ஹோட்டல்ல சுத்த சைவ சாப்பாடு கிடைக்குமா?
context: Asking a waiter before ordering.
explain: With 'does' the main verb stays in base form: 'serve', not 'serves'.
usage: Use it with a waiter or a cashier when you eat only vegetarian food.
leelaQ: What is your favourite vegetarian dish?
answer: My favourite dish is paneer butter masala with hot rotis.

en: How spicy is this curry?
context: Asking a waiter.
explain: 'How' plus an adjective asks about the degree: how spicy, how big, how old.
usage: Use it at a restaurant if you do not like very hot food.
leelaQ: Do you like spicy food?
answer: Yes, I like spicy food very much.

en: Can we get the bill, please?
context: Asking a waiter after the meal.
explain: A polite phrase used at the end of a meal. 'Get the bill' means bring the bill.
usage: Use it with a waiter at the end of a meal.
leelaQ: Who usually pays the bill when you eat with friends?
answer: We usually share the bill equally.

en: Excuse me, where can I wash my hands?
context: Asking at a restaurant.
explain: 'Where can I ...?' asks for a place to do something.
usage: Use it in a restaurant or a function hall.
leelaQ: When do you wash your hands?
answer: I wash my hands before every meal.

en: What is the Wi-Fi speed in the hotel?
context: Asking a hotel manager.
explain: 'What is the ... of ...?' asks for a fact or a number.
usage: Use it at a hotel or a co-working place if you need to work online.
leelaQ: What do you do online most of the time?
answer: I watch videos and chat with friends.

en: Are you free this afternoon?
context: Asking a colleague before a discussion.
explain: 'Are you free?' means do you have time. It is a polite way to start.
usage: Use it with a colleague, friend or a boss before asking for time.
leelaQ: What do you do in your free time?
answer: I read stories in my free time.

en: Do you want me to wait for you?
context: Asking a friend in a market.
explain: 'Do you want me to ...?' offers help or asks what the other wants.
usage: Use it with a friend or a family member when they go into a shop or an office.
leelaQ: Do you wait for friends when they are late?
answer: Yes, I wait for ten minutes at most.

en: Shall we start the work now?
context: Suggesting to a teammate.
explain: 'Shall we ...?' is a polite suggestion in British and Indian English.
usage: Use it with a team or a friend when you suggest starting together.
leelaQ: How do you start your work every day?
answer: I make a list and then start the first task.

en: What if the train is late?
context: Discussing a plan with a friend.
explain: 'What if ...?' asks about a possible problem and its solution.
usage: Use it when you plan a trip with friends or family.
leelaQ: What will you do if it rains tomorrow?
answer: I will stay at home and watch a movie.

en: How about meeting at the coffee shop at six?
tamil: ஆறு மணிக்கு காபி ஷாப்ல மீட் பண்ணலாமா?
context: Suggesting a meeting place.
explain: 'How about ...ing?' makes a friendly suggestion.
usage: Use it with a friend when you choose a time and place.
leelaQ: Where do you meet your friends?
answer: We meet at a cafe near my college.

en: Isn't it too late to start now?
context: Doubting a plan politely.
explain: A negative question like 'Isn't it ...?' shows you doubt or worry about something.
usage: Use it with a friend or a colleague to share a concern gently.
leelaQ: Do you feel it is late to learn new things?
answer: No, it is never too late to learn something new.

en: Don't you think we should call the doctor?
context: Giving advice about an unwell family member.
explain: 'Don't you think ...?' gives advice softly in the form of a question.
usage: Use it at home when someone is not feeling well.
leelaQ: When do you call a doctor?
answer: I call a doctor when the fever stays for two days.

en: Why don't we ask the teacher about it?
context: Suggesting to a classmate.
explain: 'Why don't we ...?' is a common way to suggest something.
usage: Use it with classmates or friends when you cannot solve a problem.
leelaQ: Who do you ask when you have a doubt?
answer: I ask my teacher or a senior friend.

en: I can't find my keys, have you seen them?
context: Asking a family member at home.
explain: The first part is negative (can't find). The second part is a question about a recent event.
usage: Use it at home or office when you are in a hurry and lose something.
leelaQ: Where do you keep your house keys?
answer: I keep my keys on a hook near the door.

en: I did not understand the last question, can you repeat it?
tamil: கடைசி கேள்வி எனக்கு புரியலை, திரும்ப சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Asking an interviewer or a teacher.
explain: This sentence says the problem first, then makes a polite request.
usage: Use it in an interview, a class or a meeting.
leelaQ: What do you do when you do not understand something?
answer: I ask the person to repeat it slowly.

en: I don't know where the office is, can you guide me?
tamil: ஆபீஸ் எங்கன்னு எனக்கு தெரியலை, வழி சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Asking a stranger.
explain: 'Don't know' shows a lack of information. 'Can you guide me?' makes the request polite.
usage: Use it with a passer-by or a security guard in an unfamiliar place.
leelaQ: How do you reach a new office on the first day?
answer: I check the map and leave early.

en: Nobody told me about the change, so who decided it?
tamil: மாற்றத்தை பத்தி யாரும் என்கிட்ட சொல்லலை, யாரு முடிவு பண்ணாங்க?
context: Asking in a team meeting.
explain: 'Nobody' makes the sentence negative. It is followed by a question about the decision.
usage: Use it with a team lead when plans change and you were not informed.
leelaQ: How do you like to hear about changes at work?
answer: I like to get a short message from my manager.

en: Please tell me when the next class starts.
context: Asking a classmate.
explain: 'Please tell me ...' is a polite command. The word order after 'when' is normal.
usage: Use it with a classmate or a teacher when you are not sure about the timetable.
leelaQ: What time does your class start?
answer: My class starts at nine in the morning.

en: Let me know if you need any information.
context: Offering help to a new colleague.
explain: 'Let me know' is a friendly way to offer help.
usage: Use it with a new joiner, a customer or a visitor.
leelaQ: How do you help a new person in your office?
answer: I show them around and answer their questions.

en: Tell me what you want to know about the course.
tamil: கோர்ஸ் பத்தி நீங்க என்ன தெரிஞ்சிக்கணும்னு சொல்லுங்க.
context: Inviting a student's questions.
explain: An imperative sentence can invite questions. 'What you want to know' keeps statement order.
usage: Use it as a teacher or a counsellor when someone is enquiring about a course.
leelaQ: What do you want to learn this year?
answer: I want to learn Angular this year.

en: I'd like to know the fees for the evening batch.
context: Enquiring at a training institute.
explain: 'I'd like to know ...' is a polite and indirect way to ask for information.
usage: Use it at an institute, a gym or a school office.
leelaQ: Which classes would you like to join?
answer: I would like to join a spoken English class.

en: I am calling to ask about the interview date.
tamil: நான் இன்டர்வியூ தேதியை பத்தி கேட்கறதுக்கு கூப்பிடுறேன்.
context: Starting a phone call to HR.
explain: 'I am calling to ...' states the reason for a phone call clearly.
usage: Use it at the start of a call to an office or a company.
leelaQ: Why do you usually call your friends?
answer: I call them to talk about my day.

en: I just wanted to check if you got my email.
tamil: என் மின்னஞ்சல் உங்களுக்கு வந்துச்சான்னு பாக்கணும்னு தான்.
context: Following up politely with a colleague.
explain: 'I just wanted to check' is a soft way to follow up without sounding pushy.
usage: Use it with a colleague or a client after you send a mail.
leelaQ: How often do you check your email?
answer: I check my email three times a day.
